cells.tense: Right now you can hold the whole shape of a thing without forcing it into an argument.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you noticed about this week that you haven't put into words. One sentence. Don't build a case for it.
cells.core:
You're sitting in the middle of something and you can see its whole shape. Not by assembling an argument — the read arrives before the argument does, and it usually holds up. That's rare enough that people notice it when they're near you.

What it looks like when this is working is that you're free to not know yet. You can say a thing is true without having the reasoning ready, and you don't panic when someone asks how. The next thing this can feed is structure — not the rigid kind, the kind that makes it easier for other people to stand where you're standing. You have one piece of that structure you could hand to someone who needs it.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape before you can explain it, and you're easy with that.
cells.verb: seeing what matters before you can say why
cells.place: standing inside the system with a view of the whole

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead is a version of this where you'll finally have gathered enough, and you're already living there.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you keep researching. Act on the version you have today, before you learn one more thing about it.
cells.core:
You're collecting before you move. Every unknown gets chased down, held up, filed — and there's one more angle that could make it solid. The gathering feels like seeing, but it's become the thing you're looking at instead.

What you're after sits closer than the next source. You had the shape of this before you started the file. The one thing that would help is to let the current version be enough — not perfect, just complete enough to stand on — and then do the thing. What you're really chasing is to shine from having finished something, not from having read everything. You can't finish while you're still collecting.
cells.sheetLine: You're gathering more instead of standing on what you have.

cells.tense: There's a point where you stopped treating what you saw as reliable, and you're still standing at it.
cells.ask: Say one thing you used to be sure of, out loud, to one person, before you check what they think of it.
cells.core:
You've stopped treating your read as reliable. Something you saw clearly got challenged, or ignored, or didn't survive contact with someone louder — and now you go looking for confirmation of things you already have. The search is the part that's running.

Knowledge isn't the shortage. The shortage is the willingness to move through not-knowing without demanding the whole road be visible first. You don't need to rebuild your confidence in one move. You need enough light for the next step. Say one thing you used to be sure of, to one person, without asking them whether you're right. That's not a test. It's just moving again.
cells.sheetLine: You used to see clearly. You've been asking permission for it ever since.

cells.tense: Right now you're already reading what matters, and you're calling it a hunch or a lucky guess.
cells.ask: Find one choice this week you made without a reason. Write down what you noticed before you made it.
cells.core:
You're already reading situations accurately. The read lands, and it shapes what you choose — but when you tell the story afterward, you call it instinct or chance. Your own noticing is steering decisions you describe as arbitrary.

None of that is random. You saw something and moved on it, then filed it under luck. A clear feel for what's fair and what isn't runs alongside this — you have a sense of proportion, and it mostly goes unnoticed by you. The work is small: stop describing your own read as somebody else's luck. Say what you saw, once, plainly, and let it belong to you.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading the room. Start calling that yours.
